stage_name: Real hardware-in-the-loop finding: fatal stack overflow in the S3-era persisted-state restore/migrate/save path, found and fixed via the project's first-ever real ESP32-C6 boot
note_on_commits: No new commit created; commits are only made on explicit user request. This work is uncommitted on top of 80872dc (merge of PR #49), layered on top of all uncommitted S5/S6 work including S6-tls-certificate-validation-completion.json.
sequencing_note: User connected real ESP32-C6 hardware (/dev/ttyACM0, via USB/IP passthrough into WSL2) mid-session, unprompted by any specific plan item -- the first time real hardware has ever been available in this project's history (every prior S5/S6 sub-slice was verified only via compile-and-link against the real ESP-IDF toolchain, explicitly noting 'no real ESP32-C6 hardware... available' as a standing environment constraint). User asked to flash a dev build and observe the first real boot, which immediately crash-looped; user then explicitly directed 'fix by removing the large locals from the stack (root cause)' rather than papering over the symptom (e.g. just increasing the task stack size) or merely documenting the finding without fixing it.
changed_files: components/service/persisted_state_store.cpp (changed: load()/save() each previously declared TWO ~2.2KB WireRecord locals with overlapping scope; both reduced to one, reused sequentially)
components/service/include/persisted_device_state.hpp (changed: new out-parameter overloads to_payload(state, out*)/apply_payload(payload, out*), alongside the existing by-value overloads)
components/service/persisted_device_state.cpp (changed: by-value overloads now thin wrappers around the new out-parameter overloads, which hold the real logic)

components/service/state_persistence_coordinator.cpp (changed: restore_persisted_core_state(), migrate_from_legacy_v1_blob() and persist_current_core_state() all converted from stack-local PersistedStatePayload/core::CoreState objects -- individually ~2.2KB/~2.6KB, several with 2-3 simultaneously in scope -- to function-local `static` storage plus the new out-parameter conversion calls)
frozen_decisions_applied: User's explicit instruction: fix the root cause (remove large locals from the task stack), not the two offered alternatives (increase the task's stack size as a band-aid, or merely document the finding without fixing it).

`static` (not heap allocation) was chosen for the relocated large objects, matching this project's established no-dynamic-allocation-in-service-layer discipline (check_arch_invariants.sh's INV-H002, which a same-session sub-slice had already found and respected by relocating a different module to components/app_hal rather than reaching for heap allocation) -- `static` here is architecturally justified because every affected function is reachable only from the single, dedicated `service_runtime` FreeRTOS task, gated by an atomic exchange (`consume_restore_pending()`) that prevents even that single task from re-entering concurrently with itself; verified by grepping every call site of each affected function before relying on this, not assumed.

Rather than relying on the compiler eliding large return-by-value temporaries (return-value optimization, which the real hardware crash empirically proved does NOT reliably happen at this project's -Og build setting -- confirmed by direct disassembly showing a 4800-byte stack frame surviving an initial `static`-based fix attempt that still used assignment-from-return-by-value), to_payload()/apply_payload() gained explicit out-parameter overloads that never construct a large temporary at the language level, regardless of optimizer behavior.

real_hardware_confirmed.detail: Real ESP32-C6 (QFN40, revision v0.2) confirmed via esptool.py chip_id (read-only): real factory base MAC 98:a3:16:9f:00:20. Real eFuse state read via espefuse.py summary (read-only, no --virt): Secure Boot disabled, Flash Encryption disabled, all 6 key blocks (BLOCK_KEY0-5) empty/R-W -- a genuinely blank, unburned chip. No destructive eFuse operation was performed or proposed without explicit separate confirmation, none was needed for this fix.

crash_found.status: COMPLETE -- first real boot in this project's history
crash_found.detail: First-ever real idf.py flash + boot of this firmware crash-looped roughly once per second: 'Guru Meditation Error: Core 0 panic'ed (Stack protection fault)' in the 'service_runtime' FreeRTOS task, every single boot, immediately after Wi-Fi AP + mDNS start. riscv32-esp-elf-addr2line against the real .elf pinpointed the exact crash site precisely (not guessed): service::PersistedStateStore::load() at persisted_state_store.cpp:55, called from StatePersistenceCoordinator::restore_persisted_core_state() -- a startup path that runs on every single boot, meaning this was not a rare edge case but a guaranteed, complete inability to boot.

root_cause_identified.detail: sizeof(PersistedStatePayload) measured at 2180 bytes, sizeof(core::CoreState) at 2568 bytes (both via a direct host-compiler sizeof check, not estimated) -- both dominated by a 64-entry core::kMaxDevices device array. Multiple functions in the persisted-state restore/migrate/save call chain declared TWO OR THREE of these as ordinary (stack) local variables with overlapping scope simultaneously, against the single service_runtime FreeRTOS task's 9216-byte stack budget (kRuntimeTaskStackSize, confirmed via grep, matching the crash's own reported stack bounds exactly). The worst single instance (migrate_from_legacy_v1_blob(), the legacy-schema one-time migration path) had three such objects (~2.6KB + ~2.2KB + ~2.6KB = ~7.3KB) simultaneously live -- nearly the task's entire stack budget in one function, before any caller-chain overhead.

first_fix_attempt_insufficient_real_find.status: COMPLETE -- iteratively diagnosed and resolved via real hardware, not guessed
first_fix_attempt_insufficient_real_find.detail: First fix (moving the two large locals in persisted_state_store.cpp's load()/save() to a single reused local, matching the established 'one scratch buffer, sequential reuse' pattern) was reflashed and reduced but did NOT eliminate the crash -- the device still crash-looped, now inside state_persistence_coordinator.cpp's migrate_from_legacy_v1_blob(), one call deeper on the exact same startup path. A second fix attempt (moving that function's three large locals to function-local `static` storage, reasoned to be safe given single-task/non-reentrant call graph, confirmed via grep of all callers) was reflashed and STILL did not eliminate the crash: direct disassembly of the real .elf showed the function's own stack frame was still 4800 bytes (`addi sp,sp,-704` + `lui t0,0xfffff; add sp,sp,t0` == -4096), because C++ return-value elision is not guaranteed for assignment into an existing (static) object the way it is for direct-initialization of a new one, and empirically did not happen at this project's -Og optimization level. Only the third fix -- explicit out-parameter overloads of to_payload()/apply_payload() that never construct a large by-value temporary at all, used consistently across all three affected functions in state_persistence_coordinator.cpp -- reduced the real, disassembly-confirmed stack frames to 16-48 bytes and eliminated the crash for good, confirmed by 90+ seconds of continuous stable real-hardware operation with zero panics or reboots (the longest continuous real-hardware run this project has ever observed, this being its first ever).

verification.detail: Each of the three fix iterations was verified end-to-end: host build + full ctest suite (103/103 passing throughout, no regressions at any step), cppcheck (zero findings at each step), check_arch_invariants.sh (high=0/medium=0/low=0 at each step), a real idf.py build, a real flash to the connected ESP32-C6 via esptool.py write_flash, and real serial capture of the boot log via a raw pyserial read (not idf.py monitor, which is interactive/curses-based and unsuitable for this non-interactive tool environment) with an explicit DTR/RTS reset sequence mirroring esptool's own hard-reset mechanism. The final, successful state was independently confirmed twice: once via direct disassembly of the compiled function stack frames (riscv32-esp-elf-objdump, showing 16-48 byte frames where 4800+ bytes previously existed) and once via 90+ seconds of live serial capture showing a complete, healthy boot (NVS init, Wi-Fi AP start with a real generated SSID/passphrase, mDNS start, service_runtime task start -- the line that never appeared in any of the crashing attempts -- web server start, an MQTT connection attempt that fails gracefully for the expected reason of no reachable broker on this test network, and 'Returned from app_main()') with zero panics or reboots.

real_esp_idf_build.result: PASSED (after 2 intermediate real-hardware-detected failures, both diagnosed and fixed using the real hardware itself)
real_esp_idf_build.detail: Three full idf.py build + esptool.py write_flash + real serial capture round-trips against the actual connected ESP32-C6. Round 1 (after the persisted_state_store.cpp-only fix): crash persisted, diagnosed via riscv32-esp-elf-addr2line to a different function one call deeper. Round 2 (after adding the state_persistence_coordinator.cpp static-storage fix): crash persisted, diagnosed via riscv32-esp-elf-objdump disassembly of the real compiled function to reveal a still-4800-byte stack frame caused by unelided return-by-value temporaries. Round 3 (after converting to explicit out-parameter overloads): confirmed via both objdump (16-48 byte frames) and 90+ seconds of live, panic-free serial capture -- PASSED. All build artifacts (build-hil-dev directory, sdkconfig, managed_components) cleaned up via docker run ... rm -rf after the final successful verification; dependencies.lock unaffected (confirmed via git status).

environment_note: This is the first evidence file in this project's history verified against REAL ESP32-C6 hardware rather than compile-and-link-only verification against the real ESP-IDF toolchain. Real hardware access: /dev/ttyACM0, a real ESP32-C6 (QFN40, rev v0.2) reached via USB/IP passthrough into this WSL2 environment, accessed through Docker's --device passthrough (the invoking host user lacked direct dialout-group permission, but Docker's own root-privileged device access worked regardless). All read-only recon (chip_id, espefuse summary) and all flashing/serial-capture was performed via espressif/idf:release-v5.5's own bundled esptool.py/python3 tooling inside that same Docker image, matching every other real-toolchain verification this project has used throughout S5/S6 -- only now actually executing on real silicon rather than stopping at compile/link. No eFuse burn or other irreversible operation was performed or proposed without explicit separate user confirmation; none was needed for this fix.
unresolved_deviations: The same large-struct-as-overlapping-stack-locals pattern this fix addressed in state_persistence_coordinator.cpp/persisted_state_store.cpp may exist elsewhere in this codebase (any function handling core::CoreState or PersistedStatePayload directly) -- this fix was scoped to the specific functions proven to crash (or directly adjacent to a proven crash on the very same startup call chain: persist_current_core_state() was fixed proactively since it shares the identical pattern and would predictably crash the first time a runtime state flush occurs, even though that trigger was not observed within this session's testing window). A broader audit of every core::CoreState/PersistedStatePayload call site across the codebase for the same risk has not been performed.

CoreRegistry::snapshot_copy() (components/core/core_registry.cpp) still returns core::CoreState by value with two different return statements (a pattern shown in this same investigation to be an unreliable RVO candidate at this project's -Og setting) -- left unchanged because its public signature has 11+ existing test call sites and changing it was judged more invasive than warranted for this specific, scoped fix; persist_current_core_state() (this fix's one caller of it in a stack-constrained context) now assigns its result into a `static` destination, which limits but does not fully eliminate the transient-temporary risk for that one call site.

This finding and fix is unrelated to the S6 'HTTPS and sessions' work this session was otherwise focused on -- it is recorded here as its own evidence file rather than folded into any S6 evidence file, matching this project's one-evidence-file-per-distinct-unit-of-work convention.
